lead: Low-power design keeps a CMOS chip inside its power and thermal budget. Dynamic energy falls if you switch fewer nodes, use smaller capacitance, or lower the supply; leakage falls if you cut power to idle blocks or use high-threshold transistors. A power manager applies these methods block by block. Phones, laptops and battery sensors use it; even a mains-powered router uses it to avoid a fan. This chapter covers clock gating, power gating, DVFS, multi-threshold cells and sleep modes, and their costs.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.5 for the dynamic and static power components.

sections.h3: Where the power goes, and clock gating

blocks.text: Dynamic power comes from charging and discharging node capacitance, plus a short-circuit part. Short-circuit power flows for a brief moment during a transition, when both the nMOS and the pMOS of a gate conduct and current runs straight from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground. The switching part dominates, and clock gating, power gating and DVFS all attack it. The supply voltage is the strongest knob because it appears squared.

blocks.where: α is the activity factor, the fraction of cycles a node switches (0 to 1); C is the switched capacitance in farads; V<sub>DD</sub> is the supply voltage in volts; f is the clock frequency in hertz.

blocks.text: Energy per clock cycle is E = α C V<sub>DD</sub><sup>2</sup>. One single 0-to-1 switching event on that capacitance draws C V<sub>DD</sub><sup>2</sup>. Halving V<sub>DD</sub> cuts dynamic energy per cycle to one quarter at the same activity and capacitance.

Clock gating removes edges from idle registers. An enable signal is ANDed with the clock, so a block receives no clock edges when it has no new data. The clock tree and the flip-flops then stop switching. Integrated clock-gating cells include a latch so the enable cannot change while the clock is high, which avoids a narrow glitch pulse.

items: Saves dynamic power in the clock tree and registers.
Does not cut leakage, because the supply stays on.
Costs an enable signal and a gate for each gated block.

sections.h3: Power gating, multi-V<sub>t</sub> cells and sleep modes

blocks.text: Leakage flows through off transistors. It rises with temperature and is a large share of total power in nanometre processes. Power gating places a switch between a block and a supply rail: a header pMOS to V<sub>DD</sub> or a footer nMOS to ground.

In normal mode the switch is on and the block works. In sleep mode the switch is off and the block sees no supply. The main saving is leakage while the block is off. Dynamic power in that block is already zero because it is not switching.

Costs are real. The switch adds area and resistance, so it must be sized for the block current. The block loses its state unless retention flip-flops keep it. Turning on causes a rush current that can disturb the grid, and the block cannot work until the supply settles: that is wake-up latency.

Multi-threshold cells give a second knob. A high-V<sub>t</sub> transistor has a larger threshold, so it leaks less but switches slower. A low-V<sub>t</sub> transistor is fast but leaky. Synthesis uses low-V<sub>t</sub> cells on critical paths and high-V<sub>t</sub> cells elsewhere.
Sleep modes form a ladder: clock gating (fast, small saving), state retention (keeps registers), and full power gating (largest saving, longest wake-up).

DVFS means dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. The power manager chooses a voltage-frequency pair from a table. A lower supply saves energy, but transistors get slower, so the clock must also fall. The pair must meet timing at every corner.

For a workload change from (V<sub>1</sub>, f<sub>1</sub>) to (V<sub>2</sub>, f<sub>2</sub>), the dynamic power ratio is (V<sub>2</sub>/V<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup> × (f<sub>2</sub>/f<sub>1</sub>) when capacitance and activity stay fixed.

The manager gets workload hints from the operating system, from performance counters, or from a hardware queue. It must respect regulator and PLL delays. Changing the pair too often spends more energy than it saves, so governors use hysteresis and minimum residency times.

The figure shows the control chain. The workload informs the power manager; the manager applies DVFS and gating; the functional blocks change their supply, clock or on/off state. The manager does not process data.

figure.caption: The workload feeds a power manager, which selects DVFS and gating for the functional blocks. Notice that the manager controls techniques, not the blocks directly.

spec.aria: A control chain from workload to power manager to techniques to functional blocks.

examples.question: A block runs at V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.2 V and f = 1 GHz. DVFS moves it to V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.0 V and f = 0.8 GHz. The activity factor and capacitance stay the same. Find the ratio of new dynamic power to old dynamic power and the percentage saving.
steps: Write old and new dynamic power: P<sub>1</sub> = α C (1.2 V)<sup>2</sup> (1 GHz) and P<sub>2</sub> = α C (1.0 V)<sup>2</sup> (0.8 GHz).
Divide: P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = (1.0/1.2)<sup>2</sup> × (0.8/1.0). The terms α and C cancel.
examples.answer: New dynamic power is 0.5556 times the old value, a saving of 44.4%.
examples.check:
v1=1.2
v2=1.0
f1=1.0
f2=0.8
ratio=(v2/v1)**2*(f2/f1)
saving=(1-ratio)*100
print(round(ratio,4))
print(round(saving,1))

traps: Power gating is not a dynamic-power method during normal operation; it mainly cuts leakage while a block is off.
Clock gating saves dynamic power in the clock tree and registers, but it does not stop leakage.
In P<sub>dyn</sub> = α C V<sub>DD</sub><sup>2</sup> f, the supply is squared and frequency is not; doubling V<sub>DD</sub> at fixed f quadruples dynamic power.
DVFS must lower frequency when it lowers voltage, because a lower supply makes gates slower.
A high-V<sub>t</sub> cell is not free: it leaks less but adds delay, so it belongs off the critical path.

quiz.q: State the dynamic power formula and define each symbol.
quiz.a: P<sub>dyn</sub> = α C V<sub>DD</sub><sup>2</sup> f. α is activity factor, C is switched capacitance in farads, V<sub>DD</sub> is supply in volts, f is frequency in hertz.

quiz.q: Why does clock gating not reduce leakage?
quiz.a: Clock gating stops clock edges but leaves the supply connected. Off transistors still leak, so leakage is nearly unchanged.

quiz.q: V<sub>DD</sub> falls from 1.2 V to 1.1 V and f from 1.0 GHz to 0.9 GHz. Find the dynamic power ratio and the percentage saving.
A block is power-gated and wakes once every 10 us, so the off gap is about 8 us. Wake-up takes 2 us and uses extra energy. Explain why aggressive power gating may lose here.
quiz.a: The off window of about 8 us is only a few times the 2 us wake-up time, and each wake burns extra energy plus the 2 us of lost work. The leakage saved in that short window may not cover the wake energy, so retention or clock gating wins for short gaps.

quiz.q: Why are high-V<sub>t</sub> cells used off the critical path?
quiz.a: They leak less but are slower. Off the critical path, extra delay does not set the clock period, so the leakage saving is free in timing.

quiz.q: What does DVFS stand for and which two quantities change?
quiz.a: Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. It changes supply voltage and clock frequency together.

quiz.q: When moving to a lower performance point, why lower frequency before voltage?
quiz.a: If voltage falls while frequency is still high, gate delays rise and the block can fail before the regulator settles. Lower f first, then V. When raising performance, raise V first, then f.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses power intent formats such as UPF and CPF to describe power domains, isolation cells and retention. Search for DVFS governors, power-gating rush current, body biasing and near-threshold computing. Newer flows combine power management with thermal management.
